body:
As discussed on Gitter, for Hibernate I actually rely on this behavior to implement certain "conditionally disabled" filters.  Specifically, I define annotations that allow the tester to say that a test should only be run against a certain Dialect (database), or should be skipped against a certain Dialect).  These conditions rely on the Hibernate SessionFactory having been built and available as part of `TestInstancePostProcessor`.  In order for this to work, the order has to be: 

1. instantiate the test class
2. apply and `TestInstancePostProcessor`
3. check `ExecutionCondition`(s)

@sebersole Your extension doesn't require the test instance to evaluate the condition, only the `SessionFactory`, right? Could you ensure it is built in `ExecutionCondition`, store it in the root `ExtensionContext`'s store and access it in `TestInstancePostProcessor`?

The test instance is used to provide the details needed to create the SessionFactory.  Could we do it another way?  Sure.  I'm open to suggestions.  But I just cannot see how such an approach does anything but make the tests harder to follow.
Are these details read from "static" information, e.g. annotations, or by calling a method or inspecting a field of the test instance?

The test acts as a `SessionFactoryProducer`.  The extension casts the test
instance to this and calls the single `#produceSessionFactory` method,
which in turn calls a number of protected and override-able methods to
achieve that (template pattern).  It is all instance-specific, not static.


On Wed, Nov 1, 2017 at 12:15 PM Marc Philipp <notifications@github.com>
wrote:

> Are these details read from "static" information, e.g. annotations, or by
> calling a method or inspecting a field of the test instance?
>
> —

> .
>

Is this something y'all plan on changing?  I'd rather know before I get too far down the path of migrating all of our tests to JUnit 5.  Long story short, we rely on this behavior and this behavior going away makes it questionable whether I can do the move.

As you are probably aware, an `ExecutionCondition` is evaluated once for the test class and, if that isn't already disabled, for each test method. In your case, you could keep the test class enabled but disable all tests. The evaluation of the `ExecutionCondition` for the test methods will be able to access the test instance when `Lifecycle.PER_CLASS` is used. The only downside I can see is that the condition will have to be evaluated multiple times. Would that be a problem?

body: @marcphilipp Practically speaking there should not be a problem with what you outlined *provided* the TestInstancePostProcessor has had the opportunity to inject the SessionFactory, which I assume would be the case in what you describe

> *provided* the TestInstancePostProcessor has had the opportunity to inject the SessionFactory, which I assume would be the case in what you describe

Yes, that would be the case for an `ExecutionCondition` invoked at the method level.
